cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) populations and cultivars
processing: Fresh leaf is withered briefly, pan-fired to stop oxidation, rolled by hand or machine and dried in the sun; this unsorted, unpressed leaf is maocha, the semi-finished material from which every cake, brick and tuo is pressed.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) maocha is the most valuable and reaches the market within days of picking; summer and autumn maocha follow and are cheaper.
appearance_dry: Long, loosely twisted leaves in grey-green and silver with visible stems, a few yellow flakes and some broken bits, smelling of sun and hay.
appearance_wet: Whole, supple, yellow-green leaves and buds, opening fully because nothing has been compressed.
taste_profile: Everything the origin has to offer, in its most direct form: fresh florals and honey, a clean bitterness that converts to sweetness, lively astringency when very young and a quick, open release in the cup.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, very briefly. Loose leaf opens immediately, so use a little less tea than for a cake and keep the first steeps to a few seconds; it is the easiest form of sheng to over-brew.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest season and year, and by village or garden, in bags of a few hundred grams up to the kilo lots that producers buy in April and May; the spring maocha price of a famous village is the number the whole pu-erh trade watches. It is meant to be drunk within the first year or two or pressed; loose leaf in open air ages faster and loses aroma, so 'aged maocha' is unusual and typically means a few years of sealed storage, after which it turns honeyed and soft. Nearly all maocha on sale is the current and previous year's harvest, which is why it is the best way to taste a village before buying its cake.
description:
Maocha is raw pu-erh before it becomes anything else: the sun-dried, unsorted leaf that comes out of the village processing shed and goes to market in sacks. Every cake, brick and tuo is pressed from it, and increasingly it is sold as it is, because many drinkers prefer loose leaf and because tasting the maocha is how producers decide what to press.

The process is the whole of sheng processing minus the pressing: a short wither, a hot wok to stop oxidation, rolling, and drying in the sun on bamboo mats. It is sold with its stems, its yellow flakes and its broken bits still in it, unless the producer has sorted it, and the sorted-out yellow leaves become huangpian.

In the cup, maocha is the most direct version of any origin: the florals and honey of Yiwu, the bitterness of Bulang, the sugar of Bingdao, all released immediately because nothing is compressed. The first year it is bright, grassy and sharp, and it mellows quickly in a sealed bag. The classic mistake is treating it like a cake: use a little less leaf, cooler water and very short early steeps, or the astringency runs ahead of the sweetness.

It is sold by season, year and village, from small bags for drinkers up to kilo lots for buyers, and the spring maocha market in April sets the year's prices for every famous village. Fresh loose maocha is the honest way to taste a village before paying cake prices, and the easy way to be cheated, because loose leaf from anywhere can be sold under any name. Ask for the garden, look for long whole leaves and thick stems, and judge the throat sweetness.

Store it sealed and dark if you want it to keep its aroma; if you want it to age, press it or buy the cake.
